facts.title: Named for a Homeland
facts.text: Polonium was discovered in 1898 by Marie Curie and her husband Pierre while sifting through tons of uranium ore called pitchblende from Bohemia. Marie named it after Poland, her native country, which at the time did not exist as an independent state but was partitioned among Russia, Prussia, and Austria. It was the very first element she discovered, several months before radium.

facts.title: A Sliver in a Mountain of Ore
facts.text: Polonium is staggeringly rare: uranium ores contain only about 0.1 milligram of polonium per metric tonne of uranium. The Curies had to process several tonnes of pitchblende just to isolate trace amounts, doing the back-breaking chemistry by hand in a leaky shed. Today almost all usable polonium is made artificially in nuclear reactors rather than mined.

facts.title: It Glows and Heats Itself
facts.text: Polonium-210 is so intensely radioactive that a single gram releases about 140 watts of heat, enough to glow with a faint blue light caused by the surrounding air being ionized. A capsule of it stays noticeably warm to the touch entirely on its own. This self-heating once made it a candidate fuel for compact thermoelectric power sources.

facts.title: Powering Spacecraft and Rovers
facts.text: Because polonium-210 produces tremendous heat as it decays, it was used as a radioisotope heater unit to keep equipment from freezing in space. The Soviet Lunokhod 1 and Lunokhod 2 moon rovers in the early 1970s carried polonium heat sources to survive the bitterly cold lunar nights. Its short half-life, however, limits such uses to short missions.

facts.title: The Eight-Alpha Decay Origin
facts.text: Naturally occurring polonium is a fleeting member of the uranium-238 decay chain, formed when uranium slowly transforms through a long series of radioactive steps. Polonium-210 itself is the granddaughter of lead-210 and emerges far down that chain. This means tiny traces of polonium exist anywhere uranium is found, including ordinary soil and rocks.

facts.title: Half-Life of 138 Days
facts.text: Polonium-210, the most common isotope, has a half-life of about 138 days, meaning half of any sample decays away in roughly four and a half months. It emits almost pure alpha particles, with very little penetrating gamma radiation. This makes it relatively harmless outside the body but extremely dangerous if inhaled or swallowed.

facts.title: Hiding in Tobacco Smoke
facts.text: Polonium-210 is a real, measurable component of cigarette smoke, having been absorbed by tobacco plants from soil and phosphate fertilizers. When the leaves are burned and inhaled, the polonium lodges in lung tissue and delivers a tiny but persistent dose of alpha radiation. Researchers consider it one of the contributors to smoking-related lung cancer risk.

facts.title: A Tool Against Static
facts.text: In industry, polonium's flood of alpha particles is harnessed to ionize the air and neutralize static electricity. Anti-static brushes and devices using sealed polonium sources are used to clean dust from camera lenses, photographic film, and sensitive electronics. The same alpha emission that makes it dangerous internally is safely blocked by the device's casing.

facts.title: Igniting the First Bombs
facts.text: During the Manhattan Project, polonium was paired with beryllium to build neutron initiators, the tiny triggers that started the chain reaction in early atomic bombs. When polonium's alpha particles strike beryllium, they knock loose a burst of neutrons at exactly the right instant. This urchin-like initiator sat at the heart of the first nuclear weapons.

facts.title: A Metal That Self-Destructs
facts.text: Solid polonium is a genuine metal with two crystalline forms, and it conducts electricity, yet its own radioactivity is so fierce that it can damage and disrupt its own crystal structure over time. The constant alpha decay generates heat that can melt small samples and slowly degrades any container holding it. Studying it requires sealed apparatus because even handling a visible amount is profoundly hazardous.
